title: Jacques Cartier's Voyages to the St. Lawrence
intro: Jacques Cartier, a mariner from Saint-Malo, sailed three times to the Gulf of St. Lawrence and the St. Lawrence River under commissions from Francis I of France. The first voyage hoped for a western passage to the East Indies; the later ones sought the 'Kingdom of Saguenay' and a settlement.
ending: Cartier left Charlesbourg-Royal in early June 1542 and reached France in October, on his last voyage. The settlement was abandoned in 1543, and no permanent European settlement was made in Canada before 1605.

stops.text: Cartier sailed under a commission from the king, hoping to find a western passage to the wealthy markets of the East Indies. The commission told him to find islands and lands said to hold gold and other precious things.
stops.quote: On 20 April 1534, Cartier set sail under a commission from the king, hoping to discover a western passage to the wealthy markets of the East Indies.

stops.text: After twenty days across the ocean Cartier explored Newfoundland, the Strait of Belle Isle and the Gulf of St. Lawrence. At the Islands of the Birds his crew killed around 1000 birds, most of them great auks, now extinct.
stops.quote: During one stop at Îles aux Oiseaux (Islands of the Birds, now the Rochers-aux-Oiseaux federal bird sanctuary, northeast of Brion Island in the Magdalen Islands), his crew slaughtered around 1000 birds, most of them great auks (extinct since 1852).

stops.text: Cartier met a party of St. Lawrence Iroquoians and planted a 10-metre cross reading 'Long Live the King of France', claiming the land for the king. He kidnapped the two sons of their chief, Donnacona, who agreed under pressure on condition that they return with European goods to trade.
stops.quote: His third encounter took place on the shores of Gaspé Bay with a party of St. Lawrence Iroquoians, where on 24 July he planted a cross to claim the land for France.

stops.text: Cartier set sail on 19 May 1535 with three ships, 110 men and the two Iroquoian captives, and sailed upriver for the first time. He reached Stadacona, the Iroquoian capital, where Chief Donnacona ruled.
stops.quote: Reaching the St. Lawrence, he sailed upriver for the first time, and reached the Iroquoian capital of Stadacona, where Chief Donnacona ruled.

stops.text: Using his smallest ship, Cartier arrived at Hochelaga, where a crowd of over a thousand came to the river's edge to greet the French. Rapids blocked the river and he went no further, though he believed it the Northwest Passage.
stops.quote: Cartier left his main ships in a harbour close to Stadacona, and used his smallest ship to continue on to Hochelaga (now Montreal), arriving on October 2, 1535.

stops.text: After two days at Hochelaga, Cartier returned to Stadacona and the French wintered there. The fleet froze in from mid-November to mid-April, and scurvy killed, by Cartier's estimate, 50 Iroquoians; Domagaya told him of a cure, and 85 Frenchmen survived.
stops.quote: After spending two days among the people of Hochelaga, Cartier returned to Stadacona on October 11.

stops.text: In early May 1536 Cartier kidnapped Chief Donnacona to take him to France, to tell of the 'Kingdom of Saguenay', said to be full of gold, rubies and other treasures. The ships reached Saint-Malo on 16 July.
stops.quote: After sailing down the St. Lawrence and crossing the Atlantic, Cartier and his men reached Saint-Malo on 16 July 1536, bringing the second voyage to an end.

stops.text: Cartier left with five ships, sailing ahead of Roberval, who was named lieutenant general and was waiting for artillery and supplies. The aims were now the 'Kingdom of Saguenay' and a permanent settlement on the St. Lawrence.
stops.quote: On May 23, 1541, Cartier departed Saint-Malo on his third voyage with five ships.

stops.text: Cartier anchored at Stadacona and met the Iroquoians again. He found their 'show of joy' and their numbers worrisome and decided not to build his settlement there.
stops.quote: Anchoring at Stadacona, Cartier again met the Iroquoians, but found their "show of joy" and their numbers worrisome, and decided not to build his settlement there.

stops.text: A few kilometres upriver, at the site of present-day Cap-Rouge, Cartier landed the convicts and other colonists, turned the surviving cattle loose and planted a kitchen garden. The fortified settlement was named Charlesbourg-Royal, with a second fort on the cliff above.
stops.quote: Sailing a few kilometres upriver to a spot he had previously observed, he decided to settle on the site of present-day Cap-Rouge, Quebec.

stops.text: On 7 September Cartier left with the longboats to look for Saguenay. He reached Hochelaga, but bad weather and the many rapids stopped him from continuing to the Ottawa River.
stops.quote: Having set tasks for everyone, Cartier left with the longboats for a reconnaissance in search of "Saguenay" on September 7. Having reached Hochelaga, he was prevented by bad weather and the numerous rapids from continuing up to the Ottawa River.

stops.text: Back at the fort, by Cartier's account, the Iroquoians were prowling about in a sinister manner. After the winter, from which few records survive, returning sailors said they attacked and killed about 35 settlers. Cartier left for France in early June 1542.
stops.quote: It seems the natives attacked and killed about 35 settlers before the Frenchmen could retreat behind their fortifications.

notes: Source is a biography with three voyages; all three told as legs. Stops left out: Newfoundland/Belle Isle/Chaleur Bay encounters (no precise place or date); the 1534 return and the 1542 return to France (article gives only 'France', 1534 September and 1542 October); the meeting with Roberval off Newfoundland (no named place); the second voyage's departure (port not named). Dates: 'Îles aux Oiseaux' and Stadacona 1535/1541 have no day in the article (the 1534 voyage 'starting on 10 May' explored the gulf). Gaspé: article names 'shores of Gaspé Bay'; wp set to Gaspé, Quebec. Hochelaga entry null (Montreal entry is the present city; article says Hochelaga is now Montreal); wp title 'Hochelaga (village)' is a guess at the article's title, check. Stop 'Charlesbourg-Royal' at Cap-Rouge: the 1541 stop date is the voyage year; the winter stop's year 1542 sets the end. The 1542 stop's quote is of the winter, the article says no records exist about it. The 1535 text 'by sea' for Stadacona means upriver from the gulf; 85 survivors and 50 deaths as the article gives them. The captives of 1534 and Donnacona's kidnap in 1536 are told as the article tells them; the article does not say what became of Donnacona.
